questions.q: Write the general structural formulas for a primary aliphatic amine, a secondary aromatic amine, and a tertiary mixed amine using R, R', Ar symbols.
questions.a: Primary aliphatic: RNH₂; Secondary aromatic: ArNHR' (or Ar₂NH if both aryl); Tertiary mixed: R₂NR' or RR'R''N (three different groups). A wrong answer like writing R₃N for primary reveals confusion between the number of carbon groups attached vs. number of H atoms replaced. Students often count alkyl groups instead of tracking H replacement on ammonia.

questions.q: Explain why (CH₃)₂NH is a secondary amine but (CH₃)₃N is tertiary, even though both have only methyl groups attached to nitrogen.
questions.a: Classification depends on how many H atoms of NH₃ are replaced, not on the number of distinct alkyl groups. (CH₃)₂NH has two H replaced (one H left on N) → secondary; (CH₃)₃N has three H replaced (no H on N) → tertiary. A student who says "both have two/three methyl groups so both secondary" is counting substituents instead of tracking substitution on ammonia.

questions.q: Draw the structures of all isomeric amines with molecular formula C₃H₉N and classify each as primary, secondary, or tertiary. Indicate which are simple and which are mixed.
questions.a: Four isomers: (1) CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propan-1-amine, primary, simple); (2) CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃ (propan-2-amine, primary, simple); (3) CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ (N-methylethanamine, secondary, mixed); (4) (CH₃)₃N (N,N-dimethylmethanamine, tertiary, simple). Missing the branched primary isomer or misclassifying N-methylethanamine as primary (due to –NH–) are common errors. Check that each structure has exactly 3 carbons, 9 hydrogens, 1 nitrogen.

questions.q: Compare the bond angles in NH₃, CH₃NH₂, and (CH₃)₃N. Predict the trend and justify using hybridisation and lone pair repulsion.
questions.a: All are sp³ hybridised with a lone pair. Ideal tetrahedral angle = 109.5°. Lone pair-bond pair repulsion > bond pair-bond pair repulsion, so angles < 109.5°. As bulky alkyl groups replace H, steric crowding increases, compressing the angle further: NH₃ (107°) > CH₃NH₂ (~108°) > (CH₃)₃N (108° per NCERT, but note: experimental trend shows slight decrease then increase due to steric vs. electronic balance). A student who says "angles increase because alkyl groups are larger" ignores lone pair repulsion dominance.

questions.q: A student writes: "Aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) is a tertiary amine because the nitrogen is attached to three atoms: two carbons from the ring and one hydrogen." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: False. Classification counts carbon/aryl groups directly bonded to nitrogen, not total bonds. In aniline, nitrogen is bonded to one aryl group (the phenyl ring) and two hydrogens → one H replaced → primary amine. The student incorrectly counts the two ring carbons as two separate substituents; the phenyl group is a single aryl substituent. This misconception arises from confusing coordination number with substitution degree.

questions.q: Design a flow-chart algorithm (using only yes/no questions) that takes any amine structure as input and outputs its classification (1°/2°/3°) and whether it is simple or mixed. Test your algorithm on C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂.
questions.a: Algorithm: (1) Count number of C/Ar groups directly bonded to N → if 1: primary; if 2: secondary; if 3: tertiary. (2) If secondary/tertiary, check if all attached C/Ar groups are identical → yes: simple; no: mixed. For C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂: three groups (one phenyl, two methyl) → tertiary; groups differ → mixed. A poor answer uses "count H on N" which fails for amides/imines, or forgets the mixed/simple check.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia (NH₃) in which one, two, or all three hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, classified as primary (RNH₂/ArNH₂), secondary (R₂NH/RNHR'), or tertiary (R₃N/R₂NR') based on the number of hydrogen atoms substituted; each amine retains a trivalent nitrogen with an unshared electron pair and sp³ ______ giving a pyramidal geometry.

Fill in the blank: Begin with a real-world observation: when you peel an onion, the pungent smell comes from propanethial-S-oxide, but the tear-inducing compound in chilli peppers is capsaicin — both contain nitrogen in amine-like ______ groups.
What is Amines? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia (NH₃) in which one, two, or all three hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, classified as primary (RNH₂/ArNH₂), secondary (R₂NH/RNHR'), or tertiary (R₃N/R₂NR') based on the number of hydrogen atoms substituted; each amine retains a trivalent nitrogen with an unshared electron pair.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Emphasise that the nitrogen remains sp³ hybridised with a lone pair, so the geometry stays pyramidal but the C–N–C angle shrinks slightly (e.g., ______° in trimethylamine).
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Amines?
questions.a: Students often classify amines by counting the total number of carbon atoms attached to nitrogen (e.g., calling CH₃NHCH₃ primary because "only one carbon on each side") instead of counting how many hydrogens of ammonia have been replaced.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) draw the structural formula of any amine given its classification and alkyl/aryl groups, (2) classify a given amine structure as primary, secondary, or tertiary, and (3) distinguish between simple and mixed amines with correct examples.
